title: EGD Grant Program for Peace & Value Education: Funding for Community-Led Peace, Values and Social Impact Projects
summary: Applications are open for the Educational Globale et Développement (EGD) Grant Program for Peace Value Education , a funding opportunity designed to support individuals, youth groups, educators, and community members developing initiatives that advance peace, human universal values, cooperation, dialogue, community learning, and positive social impact. The EGD Grant Program provides an opportunity for people with community-focused ideas to seek funding for projects that contribute to stronger relationships, mutual understanding, peaceful engagement, and values-based education within their communities. At the heart of the program is an emphasis on people-led and community-based action . Rather than limiting participation to established organisations or a particular age group, the program invites individuals and groups to present project ideas that can contribute meaningfully to peace and value education at the community level. Youth-led initiatives are particularly encouraged to apply. However, the opportunity is open to applicants of all ages , allowing a broad range of community members, educators, young people, and other individuals interested in peace and values education to submit their ideas for consideration. About Educational Globale et Développement (EGD) The Educational Globale et Développement Grant Program for Peace Value Education focuses on supporting initiatives that promote peace, cooperation, mutual understanding, universal human values, and community learning. Through the grant application process, EGD is seeking people-led and community-based initiatives capable of creating positive social impact. Applicants are invited to explain their project ideas, the outcomes they hope to achieve, and the ways their proposed initiatives will contribute to peace and value education within their respective communities. The opportunity therefore provides a platform for applicants to move from identifying challenges or opportunities in their communities to proposing practical initiatives that encourage learning, dialogue, cooperation, and peaceful engagement. What Is the EGD Grant Program for Peace Value Education? The EGD Grant Program for Peace Value Education is a funding opportunity for projects that contribute to peace and human universal values through community-level initiatives. The application process is designed to collect information from prospective applicants and understand: The project or initiative they are proposing; The intended outcomes of the project; How the initiative contributes to peace and value education; How the project relates to the applicant s community; The potential for the initiative to encourage dialogue and mutual understanding; How the proposed activities can contribute to cooperation and community learning; and The positive social impact the applicant hopes to achieve. Applicants should therefore be prepared to communicate not simply what they want to do, but also why their proposed initiative matters and how it could contribute to the objectives of peace and value education. What Types of Projects Is EGD Looking to Support? EGD is interested in people-led and community-based initiatives that promote peace, universal human values, cooperation, dialogue, mutual understanding, community learning, and positive social impact. This broad focus provides applicants with an opportunity to develop projects that respond to the particular needs and circumstances of their communities. While applicants should ensure their individual proposals align with the official objectives of the grant program, potential initiatives may be centred on areas such as peace and values education, community dialogue, cooperation, learning, mutual understanding, and other forms of positive community engagement. The most important consideration is that applicants clearly demonstrate how their proposed project contributes to peace and value education within their community . Key Areas of Focus Based on the grant information provided, proposed projects should align with one or more of the following broad areas: 1. Peace Projects should contribute to peaceful engagement and help create environments where individuals and communities can interact constructively. Peace-focused initiatives could involve educational or community activities that encourage understanding, dialogue, cooperation, and positive relationships. 2. Human Universal Values The program places particular emphasis on human universal values . Applicants should consider how their proposed initiative can encourage values that strengthen communities and contribute to positive interactions between people. The application should clearly explain how these values will be incorporated into the proposed project rather than simply mentioning them as general objectives. 3. Dialogue Dialogue is an important component of community understanding. Projects may seek to create opportunities for people to communicate, exchange ideas, learn from one another, and better understand different experiences and perspectives. Applicants proposing dialogue-based activities should explain what they hope participants will learn or achieve through these interactions. 4. Mutual Understanding The program seeks initiatives capable of strengthening mutual understanding. Projects can therefore consider how education and community participation can help individuals better understand one another and contribute to stronger community relationships. 5. Cooperation EGD also highlights cooperation as an important component of the program. Applicants can demonstrate how their project will encourage participants, groups, educators, community members, or other stakeholders to work together toward positive outcomes. 6. Community Learning Projects that facilitate learning at the community level can also align with the objectives of the grant. Applicants should consider how participants will gain knowledge, skills, awareness, understanding, or values through the proposed activities. 7. Positive Social Impact Ultimately, EGD is seeking initiatives that can contribute to positive social impact. Applicants should clearly identify the change they hope their project will create and explain how the proposed activities could contribute to that change. Who Can Apply for the EGD Grant? The application information specifically identifies several categories of prospective applicants. Applications are welcomed from: Individuals with ideas for projects related to peace and value education; Youth groups interested in developing community-focused initiatives; Educators seeking to contribute to peace, values, cooperation, dialogue, or community learning; Community members with ideas that can create positive social impact; and Applicants of different ages who can demonstrate the relevance of their proposed project to the objectives of the grant. Importantly, youth-led programs are encouraged . However, the program is not restricted exclusively to young people. EGD explicitly states that all ages are welcome to apply . This makes the grant accessible to a broad range of people interested in designing and implementing initiatives that support peace and values education. Strong Encouragement for Youth-Led Initiatives One notable aspect of the EGD Grant Program is its encouragement of youth-led programming. Young people and youth groups with ideas for improving their communities through peace education, values-based learning, dialogue, cooperation, and related activities are encouraged to submit applications. A youth-led initiative should clearly demonstrate the role young people will play in shaping or implementing the project. At the same time, applicants should remember that youth participation is encouraged rather than presented as an exclusive eligibility condition. Applicants of all ages are welcome. Why Community-Based Initiatives Matter to the Program The EGD Grant Program specifically highlights people-led and community-based initiatives . This means applicants should pay close attention to the relationship between their proposed activities and the community they intend to serve. A strong project description should clearly establish: The community context: Explain where or within what community the project will operate. The issue or opportunity: Identify what the project seeks to address or improve. The proposed activities: Explain what will actually happen through the project. The participants or beneficiaries: Describe the people the initiative intends to engage or benefit. The connection to peace and values: Demonstrate how the project advances peace, universal human values, cooperation, dialogue, mutual understanding, or community learning. The intended outcomes: Explain what changes, improvements, learning, or impact the applicant hopes to achieve. These elements can help demonstrate that a proposal is rooted in the community rather than being only a general idea. What Applicants Should Explain in Their Application The EGD application process invites applicants to share information about their project ideas and intended outcomes , as well as how their initiative contributes to peace and value education within their community. Applicants should therefore think carefully about several questions before submitting their application. What is your project idea? Clearly explain the initiative you want to implement. Avoid relying solely on broad statements about promoting peace. Instead, explain what activities you plan to carry out and how they will work. Why is the project needed? Consider the circumstances within your community that make the proposed initiative relevant. The connection between the identified need and the proposed activities should be easy for reviewers to understand. Who will participate? Identify the community members, young people, educators, groups, or other participants the project intends to involve. What will the project achieve? The intended outcomes should be clearly stated. Applicants should explain what they hope will change, improve, or develop as a result of the initiative. How does the project promote peace and values? This is particularly important because peace and value education are central to the funding opportunity. Applicants should directly explain how their activities will advance these objectives. What positive social impact could result? Consider both immediate and broader outcomes. For example, applicants can explain how participants may benefit from increased learning, dialogue, understanding, cooperation, or stronger community relationships where these outcomes are relevant to their proposed initiative. How to Develop a Strong Project Proposal Applicants should ensure that their proposal is clear, practical, community-focused, and closely connected to the objectives of the EGD Grant Program. When preparing an application, consider the following approach: Step 1: Identify a clear community need Start by identifying the issue, challenge, or opportunity the project will address. The project should have a clear purpose rather than attempting to address too many unrelated issues simultaneously. Step 2: Define the project objective Explain what the initiative is intended to accomplish. The objective should connect directly to peace, universal human values, dialogue, mutual understanding, cooperation, community learning, or positive social impact. Step 3: Explain the activities Describe what will actually be done. Applicants should make it possible for reviewers to understand how the proposed project would move from an idea to practical implementation. Step 4: Identify the intended participants Explain who will participate in or benefit from the initiative. This could include youth, community members, learners, educators, or other relevant groups depending on the nature of the proposed project. Step 5: Describe the expected outcomes Applicants should identify what they expect the project to achieve. Where possible, outcomes should be specific enough for reviewers to understand what successful implementation would look like. Step 6: Connect the project directly to EGD s objectives Applicants should clearly establish the relationship between their proposal and the broader goals of peace and value education. A project may have several positive community benefits, but the application should specifically demonstrate why it belongs within this particular grant program. Application and Selection Process Interested applicants must complete the official EGD Grant Application Form – Peace Value Education . The application form is intended to collect information about applicants and their proposed projects. Once applications have been submitted, all applications will be carefully reviewed . Applicants should therefore make sure the information submitted through the application form accurately and clearly represents their project idea and its intended impact. Following the review process, selected applicants will be contacted via email and provided with further information regarding the next steps. Applicants should provide an email address they actively monitor and check their inbox after submitting an application. Important Information About Selection Submission of an application does not automatically mean that funding has been awarded. EGD states that applications will be reviewed and that selected applicants will subsequently be contacted. Applicants should therefore distinguish between: Submitting an application; Having the application reviewed; Being selected; and Receiving further instructions regarding the next steps. Applicants should follow any subsequent instructions provided directly by EGD if selected. Funding Amount The information provided for the EGD Grant Application Form does not specify the amount of funding available to successful applicants . Prospective applicants should therefore avoid assuming a particular grant amount unless this information is provided directly by EGD elsewhere in the official application process. Applicants should review all information available through the official application form carefully before submission. Application Deadline No specific application deadline is stated in the information provided for the EGD Grant Program for Peace Value Education. Applicants interested in the opportunity are therefore encouraged to review the official application form and submit their application while the form remains open. Applicants should also check whether EGD provides additional deadline information or updates during the application process. How to Apply Applications are submitted through the official EGD Grant Application Form – Peace Value Education hosted through Google Forms. Applicants should carefully complete all required sections and provide accurate information about themselves and their proposed initiative. When uploading files or submitting the form, applicants should also be aware that the application notice states that the name, email address, and photo associated with the applicant s Google account may be recorded when files are uploaded and the form is submitted. Before submitting, applicants should: Review their project description carefully; Ensure their intended outcomes are clearly explained; Demonstrate how the initiative contributes to peace and value education; Check that all required questions have been answered; Verify that contact information is accurate; Upload any requested supporting materials; Review the information for errors or missing details; and Submit the completed application through the official form. Application Form: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdfMv3MopHFXtFoI_IQ18AmkIoRdc8AUKgI4IA-v2qRZkYrlw/viewform Important Considerations Before Applying Because the information currently available is relatively brief, prospective applicants should pay particular attention to the instructions contained within the official application form. Applicants should not assume details that have not been explicitly provided, particularly regarding: The maximum or minimum funding amount; Project duration; Eligible project expenses; Geographic restrictions; Nationality requirements; Whether individuals or groups require formal registration; Reporting requirements; Funding disbursement arrangements; Number of grants available; or A final application deadline. Where additional information is provided by EGD during the application or selection process, applicants should follow those official instructions. Why This Opportunity May Be Relevant for Community Changemakers The EGD Grant Program offers a potential avenue for people who already have ideas for strengthening their communities but need support to turn those ideas into action. Its focus on community-based initiatives creates space for locally relevant approaches to peace and value education. The program may be particularly relevant to people interested in: Peace and values education; Youth engagement; Community development; Community learning; Dialogue and mutual understanding; Cooperation; Social impact; Community participation; and People-led approaches to positive change. The explicit encouragement of youth-led initiatives also provides young people with an opportunity to put forward ideas that respond to issues and opportunities within their own communities. At the same time, because applications are welcomed from people of all ages, the program can potentially bring together ideas from youth, educators, community members, and other individuals with different experiences and perspectives. Conclusion The Educational Globale et Développement (EGD) Grant Program for Peace Value Education provides a funding opportunity for individuals, youth groups, educators, and community members who want to develop initiatives that contribute to peace, human universal values, cooperation, dialogue, mutual understanding, community learning, and positive social impact. The program places particular emphasis on people-led and community-based initiatives and encourages applicants to clearly explain their project ideas, intended outcomes, and contribution to peace and value education within their communities. Youth-led programs are strongly encouraged, but the opportunity welcomes applicants of all ages. Prospective applicants should focus on presenting a clear and practical project idea, demonstrating its relevance to their community, identifying the outcomes they hope to achieve, and explaining how the initiative aligns with the objectives of peace and value education. All submitted applications will be reviewed, and selected applicants will be contacted by email regarding the next steps. As no specific deadline or funding amount is stated in the information currently provided, interested applicants should carefully review the official application form and consider applying while applications remain available. title: ITU Gender Champions Programme 2027: Fully Supported Global Opportunity for Young Women Leading Digital Transformation
summary: Applications are now open for the ITU Gender Champions Programme 2027 , a global leadership opportunity for young women who are using technology and digital innovation to create meaningful change in their communities, countries, and regions. Organized by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) with support from Australia and Women’s WorldWide Web (W4) , the programme is designed to recognize and strengthen the next generation of women leaders advancing digital transformation, digital inclusion, equitable access to technology, digital skills, artificial intelligence for social good, online safety, and inclusive digital policymaking. For its inaugural cohort, the ITU Gender Champions Programme will select up to four outstanding young women between the ages of 18 and 25 . Selected Champions will have the opportunity to join an international network of experts, policymakers, innovators, and fellow changemakers, while also participating in the AI for Good Global Summit 2027 in Geneva, Switzerland, from 21 to 25 June 2027 . ITU Importantly, ITU will cover key costs associated with the Champions’ participation in Geneva, including a round-trip economy flight, accommodation, and a per diem subsistence allowance. Subject to the availability of funds, selected Champions may also receive additional support to implement or strengthen a community-level project advancing the digital inclusion, access, skills, or empowerment of women and girls. The application deadline is 15 November 2026 . About the ITU Gender Champions Programme The ITU Gender Champions Programme has been established to identify and support emerging young women leaders who are helping shape a more inclusive and equitable digital future. The initiative recognizes that technology is transforming almost every aspect of modern life—from education and employment to health, entrepreneurship, governance, communications, and social participation. However, access to digital opportunities remains unequal, and women and girls continue to face barriers to participation in technology and digital decision-making. The programme seeks to elevate young women who are already responding to these challenges. Applicants may be working in fields such as: Digital skills and digital literacy Connectivity and internet access Artificial intelligence Digital innovation Online safety and cybersecurity awareness Women and girls in STEM Digital entrepreneurship Digital health Inclusive technology Technology for education Digital public policy ICT access Community technology initiatives Technology for social good Digital rights Women’s digital empowerment ITU specifically encourages applications from young women who are using technology to create positive social impact and advance digital inclusion. Who Organizes the Programme? The programme is organized by the International Telecommunication Union , a United Nations specialized agency focused on digital technologies and global connectivity. ITU brings together 194 national governments and more than 1,000 companies and organizations in its work to advance global connectivity and digital development. The 2027 Gender Champions Programme is being implemented with support from: Australia Women’s WorldWide Web (W4) These partners will also participate in the programme’s selection process. How Many ITU Gender Champions Will Be Selected? For the first cohort of the new ITU Gender Champions Programme, up to four young women will be selected. This makes the programme highly competitive. Rather than creating a very large cohort, ITU intends to identify a small number of emerging women leaders whose existing work demonstrates meaningful potential to advance digital transformation and inclusion. ITU Age Requirement Applicants must be: At least 18 years old and no more than 25 years old at the time the application is submitted. This requirement is explicitly included in the official Terms and Conditions. Applicants outside this age range would therefore not satisfy the published eligibility condition. What Type of Young Women Is ITU Looking For? ITU is looking for young women who are already demonstrating leadership through technology. Potential applicants may include young women who are: Teaching digital skills to women or girls Expanding access to connectivity Developing digital platforms or applications Using artificial intelligence to address social problems Promoting responsible AI Building technology-based businesses or social enterprises Improving digital access in underserved communities Supporting girls in STEM Addressing online abuse or digital safety Promoting cybersecurity awareness Using technology in health, education, agriculture, climate, or development Advocating for inclusive digital policies Using data or technology to strengthen public services Supporting women entrepreneurs through digital tools Helping marginalized communities participate in the digital economy The central requirement is not simply an interest in technology. The programme is intended for young women who are using technology to create positive change . Is a University Degree Required? No specific degree requirement is stated. The official programme page and Terms and Conditions do not require applicants to hold: A bachelor’s degree A master’s degree A PhD A qualification in computer science An engineering degree A formal ICT qualification This means applicants should not assume that the programme is restricted to university graduates or professional technologists. A young woman may potentially be competitive because of practical leadership, community impact, innovation, entrepreneurship, advocacy, or technology-based project experience even if she does not have a formal technology degree. The decisive issue is whether her work aligns with the purpose of the programme. Do Applicants Need to Be Computer Scientists? No. The programme is broader than software development or computer science. ITU explicitly mentions several forms of digital leadership, including: Digital skills Connectivity Innovative solutions Online safety AI for social good Inclusive digital policy Accordingly, applicants may come from technology, policy, education, health, entrepreneurship, development, advocacy, research, communications, or other relevant backgrounds. Global Eligibility The published call does not restrict applicants to a particular nationality or region. The programme describes itself as connecting young women to a global network , and ITU states that final selection will consider geographical representation alongside diversity of backgrounds and experiences. ITU That means eligible young women can potentially apply from countries across: Africa Asia Europe North America Latin America The Caribbean Oceania The Middle East Applicants should still ensure that they can ultimately obtain the necessary documentation to travel to Switzerland if selected. What Will Selected Gender Champions Receive? The programme provides several important opportunities. 1. Participation in the AI for Good Global Summit 2027 Selected ITU Gender Champions will be required to attend the AI for Good Global Summit 2027 in Geneva, Switzerland. The event is scheduled for: 21–25 June 2027 Participation places the selected Champions within a major international environment involving technology leaders, policymakers, innovators, researchers, and other actors working on artificial intelligence and digital transformation. 2. Round-Trip Economy Airfare ITU states in the official Terms and Conditions that selected Champions will receive: A round-trip economy-class flight ticket to and from the event location. This significantly reduces the financial barrier for international participants traveling to Geneva. 3. Accommodation in Geneva Accommodation during the relevant stay will also be provided by the organizer. The precise accommodation arrangement is determined by ITU. 4. Per Diem Subsistence Allowance Selected participants will receive a per diem subsistence allowance for the duration of the stay. The exact amount is determined by ITU. This allowance is intended to support reasonable subsistence expenses associated with participation. 5. Access to International Networks Beyond travel and accommodation, one of the programme’s major advantages is access to a global network involving: Experts Policymakers Innovators Technology leaders Gender-equality advocates Digital-development professionals Fellow young changemakers The programme is designed to help young leaders amplify their impact and strengthen their leadership capacity. 6. Apply for the ITU Gender Champions Programme 2027 Applicants should submit well before 15 November 2026 rather than waiting until the closing hours. title: Princeton Winter School 2027 in Behavioral Science for Climate Action: Fully Subsidized Five-Day Programme at Princeton University
summary: Applications are open for the Princeton Winter School in Behavioral Science for Climate Action 2027 , an intensive five-day, in-person programme bringing together researchers, policymakers, advocates, organizational leaders, and practitioners interested in using behavioral science to accelerate meaningful climate action. Scheduled for January 19–23, 2027 , the winter school will take place at Princeton University in Princeton, New Jersey, USA . The programme is designed around a central challenge confronting climate policy and sustainability professionals worldwide: understanding human behavior is not enough—the critical task is translating behavioral science into interventions that actually work in communities, organizations, institutions, and policy systems. The Princeton Winter School addresses this theory-to-impact gap by combining expert-led teaching with collaborative intervention design. Participants will examine the psychological, social, political, and institutional forces that influence climate-related behavior and then apply those insights to real-world climate challenges drawn from their own professional or community contexts. A particularly important feature is that the programme is free of charge for accepted participants . Tuition and programme materials are fully subsidized, while limited needs-based support for travel and campus lodging is available to students. About the Princeton Winter School in Behavioral Science for Climate Action Climate action is often discussed as a technological, economic, or political challenge. However, achieving meaningful progress also depends heavily on human behavior. Individuals must decide whether to adopt sustainable practices. Communities must build support for new interventions. Organizations must change routines and incentives. Governments must develop policies that people understand, accept, and follow. Political and institutional environments can either encourage climate action or create barriers to it. The Princeton Winter School is built around the idea that behavioral science can help explain these processes. The programme examines why people respond to climate change in different ways and how factors such as cognition, emotions, values, identity, motivation, social influence, institutional signals, organizational structures, and political contexts shape climate-related decisions. Rather than treating these concepts purely theoretically, the winter school asks participants to apply them to concrete climate challenges. Across five days, participants move repeatedly between: Expert lectures Guided discussion Behavioral diagnosis Collaborative problem solving Intervention design Implementation planning Evaluation planning Peer feedback Final presentations The result is an interdisciplinary learning environment connecting academic behavioral science with practical climate policy and action. Princeton Winter School 2027 Dates and Location The programme website lists the winter school dates as: January 19–23, 2027 The event will be conducted in person at: Louis A. Simpson International Building Princeton University Princeton, New Jersey 08544 United States Princeton Winter Sch Participants should plan to attend the entire five-day programme because the curriculum is cumulative. Each day s work contributes to the intervention proposal developed by the participant s group. One minor scheduling point should be verified directly with organizers: the practical-information page describes January 19–23 as Monday to Friday, while those calendar dates in 2027 fall Tuesday through Saturday. Applicants should therefore rely on the final schedule and logistical instructions issued by the programme before making non-refundable travel arrangements. What Makes the Princeton Winter School Different? The programme is structured around two interconnected tracks . Learn the Behavioral Science Participants will attend expert-led lectures and discussions examining the scientific processes behind climate-related behavior. Topics include areas such as: Cognition Emotion Risk perception Motivation Values Moral obligation Personal norms Social identity Political identity Social influence Concern for future generations Institutional signals Organizational contexts Political cooperation Public support for climate measures Participants will also explore how interventions operating at different levels can be combined rather than relying on a single behavioral mechanism. Put the Science Into Practice The second track centers on the Behavioral Challenge Labs . Applicants submit a real climate-action challenge encountered in their work or community. Five submitted challenges will be selected, and each will be assigned to a small group of approximately four participants bringing together research and practice perspectives. Each group will work on the same challenge throughout the programme. With facilitator support, teams will gradually move from diagnosing the problem to designing a practical intervention. This approach is important because climate problems rarely result from one isolated behavioral barrier. Effective interventions may need to address individual motivation, social norms, institutional incentives, organizational structures, stakeholder interests, political signals, and implementation constraints simultaneously. What Participants Will Do in the Behavioral Challenge Labs The Behavioral Challenge Labs provide a structured process for turning a broad climate concern into a practical intervention. Teams will work to: Define a specific behavioral challenge. Identify the relevant population. Define the setting in which the behavior occurs. Diagnose barriers at the individual level. Examine social norms and relationships. Assess institutional and organizational barriers. Map relevant stakeholders. Identify possible intervention components. Explain how different intervention components reinforce one another. Develop an implementation pathway. Develop an evaluation approach. Examine feasibility and resource requirements. Consider equity implications. Identify potential unintended consequences. Prepare and present a final intervention proposal. This makes the winter school particularly relevant to applicants who already have a climate-related challenge they want to examine more systematically. Princeton Winter School 2027 Five-Day Programme Day 1: Understanding Individual Behavior The first day focuses on the individual processes influencing climate action. Participants will examine how: Attention Cognition Emotions Risk perception Values Motivation Personal norms can affect whether individuals engage in climate-friendly behavior. Behavioral Challenge Lab teams will use these concepts to identify individual-level barriers affecting their selected climate challenge. By the end of the day, each group should have developed a clearly defined problem and an initial behavioral diagnosis. Day 2: Understanding Social Influence The second day shifts attention from individuals to social relationships and identity. Participants will explore: Social identity Political identity Social norms Relationships Group influence Concern for other people Potential messengers Allies Sources of resistance The programme will examine circumstances in which social influence can motivate climate action as well as situations in which it may create resistance. Lab groups will produce a social-level diagnosis and stakeholder map. Day 3: Understanding Institutional Contexts Climate behavior does not occur in isolation. Organizational practices, policies, infrastructure, government decisions, and political signals can strongly shape what people are able or willing to do. The third day therefore examines institutional influences. Participants will consider how: Organizational systems Government policy Political signals Infrastructure Institutional rules Incentives Constraints affect climate behavior. Teams will then integrate their individual, social, and institutional diagnoses into an initial intervention concept. Day 4: Designing for Implementation The fourth day focuses on turning behavioral insights into a realistic intervention. Participants will consider how multiple intervention components can work together, where conflicts could arise, and what resources and partnerships implementation would require. Groups will refine their proposals through facilitated design sessions and peer feedback. Their plans are expected to address: Delivery Stakeholder responsibilities Resources Implementation Evaluation Feasibility By the end of Day 4, teams should have a full draft intervention proposal and presentation. Day 5: Behavioral Science for Climate Action Forum The final day is structured around the Behavioral Science for Climate Action Forum . Teams will present their proposals to: Other participants Lecturers Facilitators Invited stakeholders Presentations will cover the climate challenge, behavioral diagnosis, proposed intervention, implementation pathway, evaluation approach, and major constraints. Participants will receive expert and peer feedback and revise their intervention proposals accordingly. The programme concludes with a broader discussion about what enables—and what prevents—behavioral science from generating meaningful real-world climate impact. What Participants Should Learn By the end of the winter school, participants should be better equipped to define climate problems behaviorally rather than only in broad policy terms. Expected learning outcomes include the ability to: Define climate-action challenges in specific behavioral terms. Diagnose individual-level barriers. Identify relevant social influences. Understand institutional constraints. Select behavioral interventions suited to particular barriers. Combine different intervention components coherently. Develop stakeholder-engagement plans. Design implementation strategies. Develop evaluation plans. Communicate intervention proposals effectively. Participants should also leave with practical tools for analyzing future climate challenges beyond the specific project developed during the programme. Who Should Apply? The organizers welcome applicants from both research and professional backgrounds. Early-Career Researchers Graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, advanced master s students, and other early-career researchers can use the programme to deepen their understanding of behavioral science and its application to climate action. The programme may be particularly valuable to researchers working in areas such as psychology, behavioral science, public policy, environmental studies, sustainability, political science, economics, organizational behavior, communication, or related fields. The official website does not, however, restrict applicants to a particular academic discipline. Policymakers Government and policy professionals can learn how behavioral evidence can be incorporated into practical climate-policy interventions. The programme may help policymakers better understand why technically sound policies sometimes struggle to gain public participation or institutional support. Advocates and Change-Makers Advocacy professionals can explore how behavioral insights relate to communications, public engagement, mobilization, social norms, and climate-action campaigns. The application page specifically includes advocates and change-makers among the target groups. Industry Professionals Professionals working in private-sector sustainability, ESG, climate strategy, employee engagement, organizational change, and related fields can examine how behavioral science can improve sustainability initiatives and help organizations encourage meaningful climate action. Organizational Leaders Managers and organizational leaders interested in influencing workplace behavior, sustainability culture, and institutional practices may also benefit from the programme. Is the Princeton Winter School Fully Funded? The most accurate description is that the programme itself is fully subsidized , but not every participant is automatically fully funded for travel and accommodation. The registration fee is: $0 The winter school covers: Tuition Programme participation Programme materials for accepted participants. Princeton Winter Sch However, participants generally remain responsible for travel and accommodation unless financial support is specifically awarded. Travel and Accommodation Funding The programme states that limited travel stipends and campus lodging are available to students who demonstrate financial need . Financial-support applications are: Needs-based Submitted at the same time as the main winter-school application Therefore, applicants seeking funding should request it through the programme application rather than expecting a separate funding round later. The practical-information page otherwise states that participants are responsible for arranging their own lodging. Preferred-rate accommodation options near campus are identified for attendees. Applicants should therefore distinguish between: Programme cost: Fully subsidized. Travel and accommodation: Normally participant responsibility, although limited needs-based support is available to qualifying students. Meals Provided During the Programme Daily breakfast and lunch are scheduled to be provided at Princeton s Prospect House. The organizers state that vegetarian, vegan, and gluten-free options will be available. Most dinners are independent. However, the programme includes: A Tuesday Welcome Banquet A Friday Closing Forum meal arrangement Participants with allergies or specific dietary requirements are advised to communicate those needs to the organizers in advance. Accommodation Around Princeton University Participants who are not receiving campus lodging support are responsible for booking their own accommodation. The programme identifies several nearby options for which preferred rates have been arranged, including: Nassau Inn Graduate Princeton Hyatt Place Chauncey Hotel Applicants should not book accommodation until they understand whether they will receive financial support and have confirmed their participation arrangements. Travel to Princeton For participants flying into the United States, the programme identifies Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) as the closest major airport. Philadelphia International Airport and the major New York City airports are also accessible through rail or shuttle connections. Rail travelers can use the NJ Transit Northeast Corridor service to Princeton Junction and then connect to Princeton by the local Dinky shuttle train. On campus, Princeton s TigerTransit shuttle system provides transportation. Accessibility The Louis A. Simpson International Building is described by the organizers as ADA-compliant, including ramps, elevators, and accessible doorways. Participants requiring accommodations such as: Assistive listening technology Alternative-format materials Mobility assistance are asked to contact the organizers in advance. The programme s practical-information page lists December 15 as the requested date for communicating specific accessibility arrangements. Daily Schedule Sessions are expected to run approximately: 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM Eastern Time Optional networking events may take place in the evenings. A detailed schedule is expected to be provided to registered participants approximately two weeks before the programme begins. Most sessions will not be streamed or recorded because the programme is designed around active discussion and collaborative problem solving. The organizers indicate that selected lectures may instead be summarized in a public post-event report. Continued Collaboration After the Winter School The programme is intended to generate collaboration beyond the five days in Princeton. Planned follow-up activities include: Team check-ins after the school. Continued collaboration among group members. An invitation to contribute to a co-authored perspective article addressing how behavioral science can be translated into real-world impact. This component could be particularly valuable for early-career researchers and professionals seeking longer-term interdisciplinary connections. Organizers and Faculty Leadership The programme website identifies: Anandita Sabherwal — Teaching Design Co-Lead Danielle Goldwert — Teaching Design Co-Lead Elke Weber — Faculty Advisor The programme is structured around expert-led teaching and collaboration among researchers and practitioners working at the intersection of climate action and behavioral science. Application Process Applicants can access the application through the Princeton Winter School website. Princeton Winter School application page The application is hosted through a Princeton-linked Qualtrics form. Princeton Winter Sch Applicants should be prepared to explain: Their academic or professional background. Their involvement in climate action. Why behavioral science is relevant to their work. What they hope to gain from the programme. What perspectives they can contribute to the cohort. A real climate-action challenge from their work or community that could potentially be used in a Behavioral Challenge Lab. Candidates requesting travel or accommodation support should also complete the needs-based funding portion of the application. Application Deadline The application deadline is: November 15, 2026 at 11:59 PM EST. Prospective participants should avoid waiting until the final hours to apply, particularly those applying internationally or requesting financial assistance. Programme Dates The programme is scheduled for: January 19–23, 2027 Attendance throughout the full five-day programme is expected. Why the Programme Could Be Valuable Climate interventions often fail not because the underlying scientific objective is wrong, but because the intervention does not adequately account for the behavior of individuals, groups, organizations, or political institutions. The Princeton Winter School attempts to address that problem by requiring participants to analyze climate challenges at three interconnected levels: Individual: What psychological or motivational barriers influence behavior? Social: How do identities, relationships, norms, messengers, and group dynamics affect action? Institutional: How do policies, infrastructure, organizations, incentives, and political contexts enable or constrain behavior? Participants then combine these insights into interventions that include implementation and evaluation planning. That structure makes the programme especially relevant for applicants who want to move beyond general discussion of climate behavior and develop interventions that could realistically be implemented. Conclusion The Princeton Winter School in Behavioral Science for Climate Action 2027 offers graduate students, researchers, policymakers, advocates, industry professionals, and organizational leaders an intensive opportunity to examine how behavioral science can be translated into practical climate solutions. Taking place at Princeton University from January 19–23, 2027 , the five-day programme combines expert instruction with collaborative Behavioral Challenge Labs in which participants develop interventions addressing real climate-action problems. Accepted participants pay no registration or tuition fee , and programme materials are covered. Limited needs-based travel stipends and campus accommodation are available for qualifying students, while other participants should plan to cover their own travel and lodging expenses. The programme is particularly suitable for people who already encounter climate-action challenges through research, policy, advocacy, public-sector work, organizational leadership, or private-sector sustainability initiatives and want to understand how individual, social, and institutional behavior can be influenced more effectively. Applications must be submitted by November 15, 2026 at 11:59 PM EST . title: Fung Global Fellows Program 2027–28 at Princeton University: Fully Funded International Research Fellowship for Early-Career Scholars
summary: The Fung Global Fellows Program 2027–28 at Princeton University is now accepting applications from early-career scholars from around the world for a year of research, writing, intellectual exchange, and collaboration at Princeton University in the United States. Administered by the Princeton Institute for International and Regional Studies (PIIRS) , the Fung Global Fellows Program brings together a small group of exceptional international scholars to spend an academic year in residence at Princeton and pursue research connected to a common intellectual theme. For the 2027–28 academic year, the program will focus on “Democracy in Crisis?” , a research theme examining contemporary challenges to democratic governance as well as the factors that allow democratic institutions and practices to remain resilient. The program is designed for scholars who are already demonstrating strong academic achievement and significant intellectual promise but are still relatively early in their careers. Successful fellows will join Princeton s academic community, participate in intellectual discussions and seminars, and develop their research while engaging with other scholars working across different disciplines and regions. Application deadline: November 16, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EST. About the Fung Global Fellows Program The Fung Global Fellows Program was established during the 2013–14 academic year and is administered by the Princeton Institute for International and Regional Studies. Its purpose is to strengthen Princeton University s engagement with scholars from around the world and encourage research and intellectual exchange that crosses national, disciplinary, and regional boundaries. Each year, the program selects six scholars from around the world to become Fung Global Fellows. These scholars spend one academic year in residence at Princeton University, where they conduct research and participate in discussions centered on a shared research topic. The program particularly emphasizes international scholarly exchange. Fellows are not simply brought to Princeton to work individually on their own projects. They are expected to participate in the intellectual life of the program and contribute to conversations with other fellows, Princeton faculty, students, and members of the wider University community. The program also includes a public seminar series through which fellows present aspects of their research to the Princeton community. The Fung Global Fellows Program describes its fellows as exceptional international early-career scholars whose work demonstrates outstanding scholarly achievement and unusual intellectual promise. What Is the 2027–28 Research Theme? The research theme for the 2027–28 academic year is: “Democracy in Crisis?” Princeton s current call for applications describes democratic governance as facing significant pressures in different parts of the world. These include the rise of populist movements, declining trust in institutions, political polarization, disinformation, and democratic backsliding. At the same time, the program recognizes that democratic systems can demonstrate resilience. Grassroots mobilization, institutional safeguards, judicial independence, and civic renewal can contribute to the ability of democratic systems to withstand political and social pressures. The central intellectual question is therefore not simply whether democracy is declining. Rather, the program seeks research that examines the conditions under which democratic systems become vulnerable, as well as the mechanisms through which democratic institutions and societies resist erosion and renew democratic practices. Research Areas for the Fung Global Fellows Program 2027–28 Applicants are invited to develop research projects that engage meaningfully with the theme of democracy, democratic vulnerability, democratic resilience, or the conceptual foundations of democratic governance. Princeton identifies several possible areas of research, including: 1. Populism and Democratic Politics Applicants may examine the drivers, development, and consequences of populist movements and how populist politics interact with democratic institutions and political systems. Research may consider questions surrounding political representation, popular sovereignty, institutional legitimacy, political movements, or changes in relationships between citizens and political elites. 2. Democratic Norms and Institutions Another potential area concerns the erosion or transformation of democratic norms and institutions. Projects could investigate how institutions such as legislatures, courts, electoral systems, political parties, public administrations, or other democratic structures respond to political pressures. 3. Media, Technology and Disinformation The program also welcomes research examining the relationship between media, technology, information environments, and democratic politics. This could include research into disinformation, changing media ecosystems, digital political communication, technology and political participation, or the ways information influences political life. 4. Economic Inequality and Democratic Legitimacy Applicants may also explore the relationship between economic inequality and democratic legitimacy. This theme opens possibilities for research examining whether and how economic disparities influence political participation, political trust, perceptions of legitimacy, representation, or citizens relationships with democratic institutions. 5. Citizens, Civil Society and Democratic Renewal The program is interested in the strategies through which citizens, civil society organizations, and institutions defend or renew democratic practices. Research could therefore investigate grassroots movements, civic organizations, social mobilization, institutional reform, civic participation, or other mechanisms through which democratic practices are sustained. 6. The Conceptual and Normative Foundations of Democracy The program also encourages scholars to examine democracy itself as a concept. Applicants may investigate questions such as what democracy means, who democracy serves, and how democratic ideas have been imagined, contested, interpreted, or transformed across different political and cultural traditions. This means that applicants do not necessarily have to focus exclusively on contemporary democratic crises. The program explicitly welcomes both contemporary and historical perspectives . A Global and Interdisciplinary Research Opportunity One of the defining features of the Fung Global Fellows Program is its international and interdisciplinary character. Applicants may address any region of the world , and Princeton welcomes scholars working in different areas of the humanities and social sciences. This creates room for research that examines democracy from different geographical and disciplinary perspectives. For example, a scholar could potentially approach the theme through political science, history, sociology, anthropology, law, area studies, international affairs, or another relevant humanities or social science discipline, provided the proposed research has a strong relationship to the annual theme. The program aims to build a cohort in which scholars can learn from one another and develop comparative and interdisciplinary conversations about democracy, its vulnerabilities, and its capacity for renewal. What Does the Fellowship Involve? Successful applicants will spend the 2027–28 academic year at Princeton University as early-career scholars. According to Princeton s application information, the academic-year appointment is for approximately 10 months and fellows will be in residence at Princeton for the period of the fellowship. The fellowship therefore provides more than an opportunity to visit Princeton briefly for a conference or short research project. It is structured around sustained research, writing, discussion, collaboration, and participation in Princeton s academic environment. Fellows will be appointed at the rank of Visiting Research Scholar . Academic and Intellectual Activities The Fung Global Fellows Program creates an environment in which fellows can develop their individual research while contributing to a broader intellectual community. Key elements include: A full academic year of research at Princeton University. Research and writing around the annual common theme. Intellectual exchange with other Fung Global Fellows. Engagement with Princeton faculty and researchers. Participation in the intellectual life of the Fung Global Fellows Program. A public seminar series in which fellows present their work to the University community. Opportunities for interdisciplinary and comparative scholarly discussion. Exposure to Princeton s international and area studies community. The program s structure is intended to encourage scholars to think beyond their individual research projects and engage with broader intellectual questions raised by the shared theme. Who Can Apply for the Fung Global Fellows Program? The 2027–28 call is specifically aimed at early-career scholars who are already employed outside the United States . Applicants must have a faculty appointment or professional research appointment outside the United States and must normally return to their existing position at the end of the fellowship. This is an important requirement because the program is not intended primarily for people who are still completing their doctoral studies or who are currently working as postdoctoral researchers. PhD Requirement Applicants must have received their PhD or equivalent qualification generally after September 1, 2017 . The program therefore targets scholars who have completed their doctoral training but remain at an early stage of their academic or research careers. Current PhD Students Are Not Eligible Candidates who are currently enrolled in a PhD program are not eligible for the 2027–28 Fung Global Fellows Program. This means that applicants should already have completed their doctoral degree or equivalent qualification by the time they apply. Current Postdoctoral Researchers Are Not Eligible Princeton also states that candidates who are currently employed as postdocs are not eligible to apply . Applicants should therefore carefully distinguish the Fung Global Fellows Program from fellowship opportunities specifically designed for current postdoctoral researchers. Faculty or Professional Research Appointment Eligible candidates must be employed outside the United States in a faculty or professional research position. If an applicant receives an offer, Princeton requires an official letter from the applicant s current employer confirming that the scholar will be permitted to accept the offer and spend the academic year at Princeton University. What Does Princeton Look for in Applicants? The selection process considers several dimensions of a candidate s academic profile. Princeton states that fellowships will be awarded based on: The strength of the proposed research project The relationship between the proposed project and the annual research theme The candidate s scholarly record Demonstrated outstanding scholarly achievement Unusual intellectual promise The candidate s ability to contribute to the intellectual life of the program The candidate s work experience outside the United States The program is therefore not simply looking for applicants with impressive academic credentials. The proposed research must also have a clear and substantive relationship to “Democracy in Crisis?” and the applicant should be able to contribute meaningfully to the intellectual exchange among fellows. Application Requirements Applicants must submit their applications online and in English. The required application materials include: 1. This means the Fung Global Fellows Program should not be viewed as a fully remote international fellowship. Visa and International Scholar Considerations Because the fellowship takes place in the United States, international scholars should consider immigration and visa requirements as part of their planning. International and Global Scope The Fung Global Fellows Program is explicitly international in scope. The program also welcomes scholars from across the humanities and social sciences. How to Prepare a Strong Application Applicants interested in the Fung Global Fellows Program should begin preparing well before the November deadline. Step 1: Study the Research Theme Read Princeton s description of “Democracy in Crisis?” carefully and determine exactly where your research intersects with the theme. The relationship should be intellectually substantive rather than simply based on the use of words such as “democracy” or “governance.” Step 2: Develop a Focused Research Proposal The research proposal is limited to three single-spaced pages. Applicants therefore need to communicate their research question, intellectual problem, contribution, approach, and relationship to the Fung theme efficiently. Step 3: Demonstrate Scholarly Achievement The selection committee considers the applicant s scholarly record. Your CV should therefore clearly present relevant publications, academic appointments, research experience, and other evidence of scholarly achievement. Step 4: Select an Appropriate Writing Sample The writing sample should provide clear evidence of your scholarly ability. Since Princeton permits an academic article or book chapter of up to 50 pages, applicants should select a piece that demonstrates the quality, originality, analytical strength, and writing ability relevant to their academic profile. Step 5: Contact Referees Early Three referees are required. Because the referees receive an automated invitation after the applicant submits the application, applicants should approach their referees early and explain the fellowship, the research theme, and the application deadline. This is especially important because recommendation letters must be uploaded before the November 16 deadline. Step 6: Confirm Your Institutional Permission Applicants employed at universities or research institutions outside the United States should be prepared to obtain formal confirmation from their employer if they receive an offer. Successful candidates are expected to be notified by early February 2027 . Applications are reviewed by the director of the Fung Global Fellows Program and a search committee.
