title: Humanitarian AI Research Fellowship 2026 at NetHope: Remote, Part-Time Fellowship for AI Researchers and Humanitarian Practitioners
summary: Humanitarian AI Research Fellowship 2026 at NetHope: Remote, Part-Time Fellowship for AI Researchers and Humanitarian Practitioners Artificial intelligence is increasingly being explored by humanitarian, development and nonprofit organizations for tasks ranging from data analysis and program support to communications, operational decision-making and service delivery. At the same time, organizations working with vulnerable communities face particular challenges around data protection, responsible AI, governance, connectivity, localization and the practical limitations of AI systems. To address some of these issues, NetHope has launched a new Humanitarian AI Research Fellowship designed for researchers and experienced practitioners interested in examining how artificial intelligence can be used responsibly in humanitarian and development settings. The fellowship is part-time, fully remote and internationally open , and will bring together a small cohort of approximately four to six fellows. Participants will conduct independent research within one of two research streams, with guidance from the AI Fellowship Lead and periodic engagement with NetHope subject-matter experts. Applications close on October 9, 2026 , although NetHope has indicated that it may review applications and select fellows before the deadline. Applicants are therefore encouraged to submit early. About the NetHope Humanitarian AI Research Fellowship The Humanitarian AI Research Fellowship is a short-term research initiative intended to expand the number of researchers and practitioners who understand the opportunities, limitations and risks associated with artificial intelligence in humanitarian and development work. Rather than focusing solely on theoretical AI research, the fellowship is intended to generate findings that humanitarian organizations, nonprofit organizations and other practitioners can use in real-world settings. NetHope says the research will focus on practical questions around AI adoption, governance, safety, localization and technical implementation. The fellowship therefore sits at the intersection of artificial intelligence, humanitarian action, nonprofit technology, responsible AI and international development . NetHope brings together humanitarian, development and conservation organizations around technology-related challenges. Its network includes more than 60 member organizations working across more than 190 countries, alongside collaboration with more than 70 technology companies. The new fellowship builds on NetHope s wider work around responsible technology and AI. The organization has been developing AI-related toolkits, research and initiatives aimed at helping nonprofits understand and responsibly implement emerging technologies. Key Details at a Glance Organization: NetHope Opportunity: Humanitarian AI Research Fellowship Format: Fully remote Work arrangement: Part-time Time commitment: Approximately 10 hours per week Fellowship period: Mid-November 2026 through February 2027 Expected cohort: Approximately 4–6 fellows Location: Internationally open Stipend: Provided to fellows; the exact amount is not publicly listed Research areas: AI Adoption Governance; AI Systems Localization Authorship: Fellows receive named authorship on published research Application deadline: October 9, 2026 Early selection: NetHope may select fellows before the application deadline What Will Humanitarian AI Research Fellows Work On? The fellowship has two parallel research streams . Applicants should have a background that aligns with one of these areas. Stream 1: AI Adoption and Governance The first research stream focuses on understanding how humanitarian and nonprofit organizations are actually adopting artificial intelligence, how they govern its use and how they manage the risks associated with AI. The work is intended to go beyond general discussions about responsible AI by examining what happens inside organizations when AI tools are introduced into real operational and program environments. Possible areas of research include: Documenting real-world experiences of humanitarian and nonprofit organizations integrating AI into their operations and programs. Examining how organizations assess their readiness for AI adoption. Understanding how AI adoption occurs at the level of individual implementing partners. Comparing different organizational approaches to AI adoption. Examining direct partnerships with AI vendors. Studying open-source and internally developed AI systems. Examining the use of commercially available, off-the-shelf AI tools. Identifying the factors that influence an organization s choice of AI approach. Identifying major AI safety and governance risks within humanitarian organizations. Exploring approaches for identifying and mitigating AI-related risks. Examining incident-response practices associated with AI systems. Developing case studies that capture useful or cautionary lessons from organizations using AI. Fellows working in this stream are expected to develop at least two case studies examining how humanitarian or nonprofit organizations are adopting, governing and managing risks around AI tools. Who fits Stream 1? This stream is particularly relevant to people with backgrounds in: Policy Program evaluation Humanitarian systems International development Nonprofit operations Organizational change Technology adoption AI governance Responsible technology Experience with technology adoption or organizational change is considered an advantage. Stream 2: AI Systems and Localization The second stream takes a more technical approach. It focuses on AI systems that can operate effectively in humanitarian environments where factors such as limited connectivity, local language requirements, resource constraints and offline access may affect how technology can be deployed. This is particularly relevant because humanitarian operations do not always take place in environments with reliable high-speed internet, powerful computing infrastructure or access to the latest proprietary AI platforms. Potential research activities include: Evaluating open-source AI models for humanitarian applications. Evaluating open-weight AI models. Assessing localized AI models. Examining fine-tuned AI models for humanitarian use cases. Comparing open or locally deployed AI systems with closed proprietary systems. Studying the risks associated with different AI deployment approaches. Examining the advantages and limitations of localized AI systems. Identifying practical AI applications for resource-constrained environments. Identifying gaps in organizational readiness for AI deployment. Developing a small collection of simple, user-friendly AI tools. Contributing to libraries of supervised fine-tuning prompts. Contributing datasets for humanitarian AI applications. This stream is therefore particularly suited to applicants with technical expertise who are interested in applying AI to real-world humanitarian problems rather than focusing exclusively on laboratory or commercial applications. Who fits Stream 2? Applicants are expected to have backgrounds in areas such as: Computer science Machine learning Applied data science Artificial intelligence AI evaluation Data analysis Model testing AI safety Knowledge of or interest in the humanitarian sector is relevant, while experience with model evaluation or red teaming is an additional advantage. Research Standards and Responsible AI Requirements Because the fellowship involves research connected to humanitarian organizations and potentially affected communities, fellows will be expected to follow established research, data protection and AI governance requirements. For example, case studies involving NetHope members or partners require appropriate consent. NetHope will also review findings before publication. Fellows will be required to follow NetHope s AI Policy, including completing an AI Disclosure Form before beginning the fellowship. They must also follow NetHope s Data Protection Policy. Where research involves personal information or affected communities, the research must comply with applicable data protection and research ethics requirements. These requirements mean that applicants should be comfortable handling research information responsibly and understanding that humanitarian AI research can involve sensitive operational and community-related information. Fellowship Duration and Workload The fellowship is designed as a part-time commitment rather than a full-time position. Selected fellows are expected to contribute approximately 10 hours per week . The fellowship is scheduled to run from approximately mid-November 2026 through February 2027 . This structure allows researchers and experienced practitioners to participate while continuing other professional, academic or research activities, subject to their ability to meet the fellowship s research commitments. The expected cohort size is relatively small, with approximately 4 to 6 fellows selected. What Support Will Fellows Receive? Fellows will conduct independent research within their selected stream, but they will not be completely isolated. The fellowship provides guidance from the AI Fellowship Lead , together with periodic check-ins and engagement with NetHope subject-matter experts. This structure is intended to provide researchers with access to sector knowledge while allowing them to take responsibility for their own research projects. The fellowship also provides an opportunity to work on research that can potentially be used by NetHope member organizations and the wider nonprofit community. Stipend and Research Authorship The fellowship provides a stipend in recognition of fellows time and contributions . However, NetHope has not publicly stated the exact stipend amount. The available fellowship information says that stipend details will be provided to selected fellows and included in the fellowship agreement. Another significant feature is research authorship. Fellows will receive named authorship credit on published research arising from the fellowship. This can provide researchers and practitioners with an opportunity to contribute to published work related to responsible AI, humanitarian technology and nonprofit innovation. Applicants should also understand that NetHope will own the research outputs and associated intellectual property, including relevant datasets, prompts, tools and code. Release and licensing arrangements will be specified in the fellowship agreement. Who Should Apply? NetHope says it is looking for mid-career to seasoned practitioners who have strong writing and analytical abilities and a genuine interest in the role of responsible AI in humanitarian impact. The opportunity is therefore not presented primarily as an entry-level AI internship. Applicants should be able to demonstrate that they can independently investigate a research question, analyze information, communicate findings clearly and complete a research project within a defined timeframe. Across both research streams, applicants should demonstrate: Strong written communication. Strong analytical skills. Ability to work independently. Ability to manage an independent research project. Ability to work within a fixed research timeline. Genuine interest in responsible AI. Interest in humanitarian, nonprofit or development applications of technology. Application Requirements According to the published fellowship information, applicants should prepare several components for their application. 1. Curriculum Vitae Applicants should submit a CV that clearly demonstrates their relevant professional, research, analytical, technical or humanitarian experience. The CV should make it easy for reviewers to identify experience related to the selected research stream. 2. Letter of Interest The application requires a letter of interest addressing several questions. Applicants are asked to explain: Motivation and relevant experience Applicants should describe their motivation for participating in the fellowship, relevant experience and interest in humanitarian and nonprofit work. AI risk in the humanitarian sector Applicants should identify one significant concern or risk associated with AI in humanitarian work and briefly explain a possible mitigation approach. Real-world AI experience Applicants should discuss an AI tool they have actually used or evaluated in a real project , rather than simply demonstrating or experimenting with it. They should explain one way the AI tool underperformed in the actual context where it was used and how they identified the problem. Applicants are specifically advised not to disclose confidential information belonging to employers or clients. 3. Professional References Applicants should provide two to three professional references . These should ideally be people who can speak credibly about the applicant s professional abilities, research skills, analytical work, technical experience or ability to work independently. 4. Optional Writing Sample A writing sample may also be submitted. A strong writing sample could help demonstrate the applicant s ability to analyze a subject, conduct research and communicate findings clearly. Important Selection Requirement: OFAC Screening All selected fellows must pass an OFAC screening before starting the fellowship . This is a condition of participation and should be taken into consideration by applicants from all locations. The fellowship is described as internationally open, but international openness does not remove the requirement to satisfy NetHope s screening and compliance requirements. Is the Fellowship Open Internationally? Yes. The opportunity is explicitly described as internationally open and remote , meaning applicants are not restricted to a particular country or continent based on the published eligibility information. Applicants can therefore apply from different parts of the world, provided they meet the professional requirements and the fellowship s screening and compliance conditions. The announcement does not specify a particular race, ethnicity or nationality as an eligibility requirement . It is also not presented as an opportunity restricted to applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America or another particular continent. However, all selected fellows must pass the required OFAC screening before beginning the fellowship. What Makes an Application Relevant to the Fellowship? Applicants should make a clear connection between their experience and one of the two research streams. For example, someone applying to AI Adoption Governance could emphasize experience involving: Policy research Program evaluation Technology adoption Organizational change Humanitarian programs International development AI governance Responsible technology Research and report writing Data protection Risk assessment Someone applying to AI Systems Localization could emphasize: Machine learning Artificial intelligence Data science Model evaluation AI testing Dataset development Prompt engineering Fine-tuning AI safety Red teaming Open-source AI Localized AI applications Technical research The strongest applications are likely to demonstrate not simply an interest in AI, but an ability to analyze how AI performs in real environments and communicate practical findings . Why the Humanitarian Context Matters AI systems that work well in well-connected commercial environments may face different challenges when deployed in humanitarian settings. Humanitarian organizations may operate in environments affected by: Limited internet connectivity Limited computing resources Data protection concerns Sensitive personal information Multiple languages Local cultural contexts Emergency situations Resource constraints Unreliable infrastructure Requirements for responsible use of technology NetHope s own research has highlighted gaps in AI governance relevant to nonprofit organizations, including issues around humanitarian principles, data protection in low-infrastructure settings and relationships between funders and organizations receiving funding. The fellowship therefore creates an opportunity to examine these issues through practical research rather than treating AI governance as a purely theoretical subject. Important Dates Application Deadline October 9, 2026 Applicants should be aware that NetHope may review applications and select fellows before the stated closing date because of the anticipated volume of applications. Fellowship Period Mid-November 2026 through February 2027 Weekly Commitment Approximately 10 hours per week Expected Cohort 4–6 fellows How to Apply Applicants should prepare their CV, letter of interest, professional references and, if available, a relevant writing sample. The application should clearly identify the applicant s motivation, relevant experience, understanding of responsible AI and experience using or evaluating an AI tool in a real project. The official announcement and application links should be checked before submitting, particularly because NetHope may make selections before the October 9 deadline. For Official information visit NetHope Conclusion The NetHope Humanitarian AI Research Fellowship 2026 is a short-term, part-time research opportunity focused on the practical use of artificial intelligence in humanitarian and nonprofit settings. The fellowship offers two distinct directions. The AI Adoption Governance stream examines how organizations introduce AI, manage organizational change and address associated safety and governance risks. The AI Systems Localization stream focuses more heavily on evaluating AI systems and developing practical approaches for localized, offline and low-connectivity environments. The fellowship is scheduled for approximately mid-November 2026 through February 2027 and requires around 10 hours of work per week. Selected fellows will receive a stipend, guidance from NetHope s AI Fellowship Lead and subject-matter experts, and named authorship on published research. The opportunity is remote and internationally open , with no specific race, nationality or continent identified as an eligibility restriction in the published requirements. However, applicants must meet the relevant professional requirements for their chosen stream and selected fellows must pass OFAC screening before beginning. With applications closing on October 9, 2026 , prospective applicants should prepare their materials early, particularly because NetHope may make selections before the official deadline. Pinto (L’76) Fellowship , an opportunity for Georgetown University Law Center graduates interested in international human rights advocacy and litigation. title: Breakthrough Energy Fellows 2027: Full-Time Climate Innovation Fellowship and Funding for Global Innovators
summary: Breakthrough Energy Fellows 2027: Full-Time Climate Innovation Fellowship and Funding for Global Innovators The Breakthrough Energy Fellows program is a global opportunity designed to accelerate early-stage climate technology innovation and help scientists, engineers, entrepreneurs, and business professionals develop solutions capable of addressing some of the world’s most difficult climate challenges. The program is part of Breakthrough Energy Discovery , the early-stage innovation arm of Breakthrough Energy, which supports climate technologies from discovery through development and toward commercialization. For the 2027 Cohort 7 , the program is seeking applications for its Innovator Fellowship, while Business Fellows and Explorers are considered through different recruitment or application processes. The Innovator Fellowship is a full-time, one-year commitment intended for innovators developing very early-stage climate technologies with significant potential to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions or address climate adaptation. Applications for the Innovator Fellowship begin with a Concept Paper and preliminary information , with submissions accepted until November 2, 2026 . Successful applicants will progress through additional stages before the 2027 cohort begins in September 2027. What Is the Breakthrough Energy Fellows Program? Breakthrough Energy was founded in 2015 as a global organization focused on accelerating the transition toward a clean-energy future. Its work addresses climate challenges through technology, policy, markets, investment, philanthropy, and other initiatives. The organization focuses on reducing emissions from five major areas: Manufacturing Electricity Agriculture Transportation Buildings Breakthrough Energy Discovery serves as the organization s early-stage innovation platform. It focuses specifically on pre-venture climate technologies and supports innovators through funding, technical assistance, networks, and other resources. The Breakthrough Energy Fellows program is designed to address barriers that often prevent promising climate technologies from progressing beyond the earliest stages of development. The program provides support to scientists, innovators, entrepreneurs, and business professionals working to transform breakthrough climate technologies into scalable solutions. Each year, the program supports two principal categories of Fellows: Innovator Fellows – scientists, engineers, and innovators developing breakthrough climate technologies. Business Fellows – experienced business professionals who help Innovator Fellows commercialize their technologies. There is also an Explorer Program , which provides funding for even earlier-stage research and technology development. Breakthrough Energy Fellows 2027 Application Deadline The key deadline for the 2027 Innovator Fellowship is: Application deadline: November 2, 2026 Applicants begin by submitting a Concept Paper and preliminary information. Selected Concept Papers progress to the full application stage, after which shortlisted applicants may be invited for a Deep-Dive interview. The Cohort 7 program begins in September 2027 . The timeline is specifically applicable to the Innovator Fellowship . Business Fellows and Explorers follow different recruitment or selection timelines. Breakthrough Energy Fellows Program Pathways The program offers several pathways depending on the stage and nature of the applicant s work. 1. Innovator Fellowship The Innovator Fellowship is the flagship pathway. It is intended for very early-stage climate technology companies and innovators who need technical de-risking, commercialization support, and resources to move their technology toward market. The Fellowship is a full-time, one-year program focused on helping innovators achieve important technical and commercialization milestones. Innovator projects typically: Are at Technology Readiness Level 1–4. Have demonstrated the potential to reduce or capture greenhouse-gas emissions at scale. Typically have raised less than $2 million in dilutive funding. Must be legally incorporated before the program begins in September 2027. Applicants do not have to have incorporated a company at the time of application. However, selected Innovator Fellows must have an incorporated company before the September 2027 program start date. The program generally targets innovators who are prepared to devote their professional efforts to developing and scaling their climate technology. 2. Business Fellowship The Business Fellowship is designed for experienced professionals who can help climate technology innovators move their technologies toward commercialization. Business Fellows work alongside Innovator Fellows and may contribute to areas such as: Go-to-market strategies Customer discovery Business models Market development Technology commercialization Industry strategy Rapid scale-up Business development The program is aimed at professionals with significant experience in relevant business and technology environments, particularly those with experience accelerating hardware technologies toward market and applicable experience in the climate sector. Unlike the Innovator application process, Business Fellows are currently recruited on an as-needed basis . Breakthrough Energy identifies gaps in business expertise among its Innovator teams and may reach out to potential candidates through its Interest Form or network. Business Fellows receive: An industry-competitive living stipend The freedom to work anywhere globally Access to industry experts and leading organizations Opportunities to contribute to the commercialization of early-stage climate technologies Access to mentors, policy experts, investors, technologists, government entities, and industry partners. The Business Fellowship is also a full-time commitment. 3. Explorer Program The Explorer Program is intended for technologies that are even earlier in development than those targeted by the Innovator Fellowship. Explorers typically work on high-risk, novel climate technologies in university laboratories or research institutions. They may continue working in their existing academic or research positions while developing their technology. Explorer projects generally fall within Technology Readiness Level 0–2 . This makes the Explorer pathway particularly relevant to researchers who have an early-stage technological concept that requires further technical exploration before it is ready to become a commercial venture. Explorers receive approximately: $50,000–$250,000 in funding Support for laboratory and office space Equipment and supplies Technical consultants Personnel Access to Breakthrough Energy s network Access to mentors, policy experts, investors, technologists, and government entities Opportunities to attend selected Breakthrough Energy events Explorers generally work with the program for approximately one year. Who Can Apply for the Breakthrough Energy Fellows Program? Breakthrough Energy Fellows is a global program and accepts applications from around the world. The program states that its communication and curriculum are currently conducted in English. The eligibility requirements depend on the particular pathway. Innovator Fellowship Eligibility Innovator applicants are generally expected to be developing a very early-stage hard-tech climate company or technology. Key criteria include: Technology Readiness Level Successful Innovator applicants typically have technologies at TRL 1–4 . The program is looking for technologies that have moved beyond purely theoretical research and have supporting data demonstrating progress toward practical application. Climate Impact The technology should have the potential, at scale, to reduce or capture at least 500 million tons of greenhouse-gas emissions per year , or meaningfully address climate adaptation. Funding Stage Innovator projects typically have raised less than $2 million in dilutive funding . This includes investment through equity, notes, and SAFEs, while grant funding does not count toward the same limit. Company Incorporation Applicants do not have to already have a company when they apply. However, successful Innovator Fellows must have a legally incorporated company before the Fellowship begins in September 2027 . Full-Time Commitment Innovator Fellows are expected to devote themselves full-time to developing and scaling their startup. They should not have external employment, consulting commitments, or enrollment in academic programs outside their startup company during the Fellowship. Professors, faculty members, and full-time researchers can apply, but they cannot remain in their existing positions while serving as Innovator Fellows. Those who need to maintain their current research positions may instead be better suited to the Explorer pathway. What Technologies Does Breakthrough Energy Look For? Breakthrough Energy is looking for breakthrough climate technologies , rather than incremental improvements to existing solutions. The technology should have the potential to make a major difference in greenhouse-gas reduction or climate adaptation when deployed at scale. The program s focus encompasses five major areas: Manufacturing Electricity Transportation Food and Agriculture Buildings However, applicants are not restricted exclusively to these categories. Breakthrough Energy also welcomes high-impact technologies in other areas when they meet the program s emissions-impact threshold. The organization emphasizes innovations that represent a step-change improvement over incumbent technologies rather than technologies that merely make incremental improvements. What Funding Does the Innovator Fellowship Provide? Selected Innovator Fellows can receive up to $500,000 in catalytic investment through a SAFE . The funding can support research and development expenses associated with achieving defined technical milestones. Eligible uses can include: Laboratory space Office space Equipment Supplies Technical consultants Staffing Other research and development expenses The program does more than provide financial resources. Fellows also receive active support intended to help reduce technical and commercialization risks. Other Benefits of the Breakthrough Energy Fellows Program In addition to funding, Innovator Fellows receive access to a broad support ecosystem. Benefits include: Active Technology Project Management Breakthrough Energy works alongside Fellows to help manage technology projects, reduce failure risks, and accelerate progress toward defined milestones. Global Network Fellows gain access to a network involving professionals and organizations across: Business Policy Government Technology Finance Mentorship and Curriculum The Fellowship includes curriculum and one-on-one mentorship intended to help Fellows develop new skills and strengthen their ability to build and commercialize their technologies. In-Kind Support Significant in-kind support may also be provided in areas such as: Communications Policy Legal matters Techno-economics Recruitment Is the Breakthrough Energy Fellowship Fully Remote? Applicants do not have to relocate to participate. Innovator Fellows can remain in their current location, although the program may organize periodic in-person events and collaboration opportunities. Fellows may receive financial resources to help offset travel costs associated with the program. The same general arrangement applies to Business Fellows and Explorers, with no mandatory relocation requirement stated for those pathways. However, applicants should distinguish between location flexibility and time commitment . Innovator and Business Fellow positions are full-time commitments. Can International Applicants Apply? Yes. The Breakthrough Energy Fellows program explicitly accepts applicants from around the world . This means applicants do not have to be citizens of the United States or another specific country to participate. The program currently conducts its communications and curriculum in English . International applicants should therefore ensure they can participate effectively in an English-language program. Can Applicants Apply as a Team? Yes. Innovator applicants who have co-founders are encouraged to apply together as a team. However, teams should submit only one application per team , and applicants are discouraged from creating a team solely for the purpose of applying to the Fellowship. Applicants who have already established a company may also apply. Those who have not yet formed a company may apply as well, provided that selected Innovator Fellows incorporate their company before the program begins. How Are Innovator Fellowship Applications Evaluated? Innovator Fellowship applications are reviewed by technical experts. The main evaluation criteria include: Technical innovation and feasibility Breakthrough potential Project plan During the selection process, applicants may be invited to participate in a virtual or in-person meeting. Applications also undergo business and legal due diligence, and applicants may be asked to provide additional information. This means applicants should be prepared to clearly explain both the technology itself and the plan for developing it. Breakthrough Energy Fellows 2027 Application Process For the Innovator Fellowship, the application process consists of several stages. Step 1: Submit a Concept Paper Applicants first submit a Concept Paper and preliminary information . The deadline for the 2027 Cohort 7 Concept Paper is: November 2, 2026 Step 2: Full Application Applicants whose Concept Papers are selected will be invited to submit a more comprehensive Full Application containing additional information. Step 3: Deep-Dive Interview Selected Full Applications will progress to a Deep-Dive interview session . Step 4: Selection Fellows are expected to be selected in mid-2027. Step 5: Fellowship Begins The Cohort 7 Fellowship begins in September 2027 . The Innovator Fellowship itself involves 12 months of advancing key technical milestones, followed by approximately three additional months dedicated to close-out and evaluation. What Happens During the Fellowship? The Fellowship is structured around the development and commercialization of climate technologies. Innovator Fellows are expected to: Participate actively in Fellowship events. Work collaboratively with other Fellows. Provide progress updates to program staff. Participate in technology management meetings. Track progress against technical milestones. Participate in formal reviews. Provide periodic reporting. Engage professionally with the broader Breakthrough Energy community. Pasted text Active Technology Management is an important part of the program. This includes monthly meetings with the program team to review milestones and budgets, a formal semi-annual review, and periodic reporting. What Happens After the Fellowship? After completing the program, Fellows become part of the Breakthrough Energy Fellows alumni community. Alumni continue to have access to: The resource portal Curriculum Events Mentors Resources through the Breakthrough Energy Network Breakthrough Energy also works with Fellows during the program to identify an appropriate path for their technology venture after the Fellowship. The organization anticipates that many Fellows will pursue commercialization and fundraising following the program. Southeast Asia Innovator Fellowship Breakthrough Energy also operates a regional partnership focused on Southeast Asia. The Southeast Asia Innovator Fellowship was established through a partnership with Enterprise Singapore and Temasek to advance early-stage climate technology companies in Singapore and the wider Southeast Asian region. SEA Innovators remain part of the global cohort and have access to the same core: Curriculum Network opportunities Technology management guidance Company-building support They also receive access to local resources and commercialization mentorship in Singapore. Applicants based in Southeast Asia participate through the SEA program while remaining connected to the wider global Fellows ecosystem. Weston Breakthrough Fellowship Another regional pathway is the Weston Breakthrough Fellowship , a partnership between Wittington Ventures and Breakthrough Energy Discovery. This initiative supports early-stage Canadian innovators , initially with a focus on agriculture. Canadian innovators working on early-stage climate technologies can apply through the regular cohort application. There are no additional special forms or submission requirements outside the standard cohort application. Selected Weston Breakthrough Fellows can receive a combined total of $500,000 in funding from the participating organizations. Explorer Program Funding and Requirements The Explorer Program is particularly relevant to researchers who are working on climate technology that is still at a very early stage. Explorers may remain employed by their existing institutions while working on their projects. The program seeks technologies at Technology Readiness Level 0–2 , making it earlier-stage than the Innovator Fellowship. Explorer funding is approximately $50,000–$250,000 and can support: Laboratory space Office space Equipment Supplies Technical consultants Personnel Explorers also gain access to the Breakthrough Energy network and selected events. The funding period is approximately one year, with milestones and deadlines established between the Explorer and the Breakthrough Energy Fellows team. Important Considerations Before Applying Prospective applicants should carefully assess which Fellowship pathway corresponds to the maturity of their technology. Innovator Fellowship Consider this pathway if you: Have an early-stage climate technology. Are around TRL 1–4. Have supporting data. Are pursuing commercialization. Are prepared to work full-time on the venture. Have typically raised less than $2 million in dilutive investment. Explorer Program Consider the Explorer pathway if you: Are working on a very early-stage technology. Are around TRL 0–2. Are still conducting research or proof-of-concept development. Need to retain your current academic or research position. Need funding to advance the technology before commercialization. Business Fellowship This pathway is intended for experienced business professionals who can help Innovator Fellows with commercialization, market development, customer discovery, business strategy, and related activities. Important Warning for Applicants Breakthrough Energy warns applicants about scams and phishing attempts. According to the program information, Breakthrough Energy does not conduct official business through social media and will not ask applicants to make payments using cash, gift cards, wire transfers, or cryptocurrency. Applicants should therefore exercise caution when receiving unsolicited messages claiming to represent the organization. title: EvEx Policy Fellowship 2026–2027: Funded Policy Fellowship for UK Public and Civil Servants to Work With Leading Academic Experts
summary: The EvEx Policy Fellowship is a funded professional development and knowledge-exchange opportunity designed to bring public and civil servants together with academics and experts from universities and research organisations. The programme gives participants dedicated time to explore real-world policy challenges, access specialist research expertise, strengthen their professional networks and develop evidence-informed approaches to their work. The fellowship is particularly focused on strengthening connections between policy professionals and the research community . Selected fellows will have the opportunity to spend up to five days in person at a university or universities between December 2026 and May 2027 , with the fellowship programme tailored around their individual or team policy needs. Applications are open to eligible individual public and civil servants as well as small teams of between two and five people who are working on the same policy challenge. The EvEx Policy Fellowship is funded through the EvEx project , which forms part of the Policy to Research programme of work . The project is funded by the Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC) and delivered through a consortium of universities. About the EvEx Policy Fellowship The EvEx Policy Fellowship has been developed to create stronger links between people working in public service and researchers with relevant academic expertise. Public and civil servants regularly encounter complex policy problems that require evidence, specialised knowledge, data analysis and collaboration across different sectors. At the same time, universities and research organisations contain significant expertise that can help policymakers understand these challenges from different perspectives. The EvEx Policy Fellowship creates a structured opportunity for these two groups to work together. Rather than being a traditional academic scholarship or classroom-based programme, the fellowship is centred around real policy challenges faced by public and civil servants . Fellows will work with the EvEx team and their university hosts to develop a programme that responds to their specific professional needs. This could involve discussions with individual academics, cross-disciplinary roundtables, university seminars, research resources and networking opportunities with other public and civil servants. The overall objective is to help participants make better use of research and academic expertise in their policy work while also developing their professional skills and networks. What Is the EvEx Policy Fellowship Designed to Achieve? The programme is designed around several key objectives. 1. Connecting policymakers with academic expertise One of the central features of the EvEx Policy Fellowship is the opportunity to engage directly with academics whose research is relevant to a fellow s policy challenge. Participants can discuss their questions, explore existing research and gain subject-specific knowledge that may be useful in their professional work. Depending on the policy challenge, discussions may take place with: Individual academic researchers Researchers from different disciplines Groups of academics Cross-disciplinary research teams Other experts within participating universities This approach allows fellows to explore policy questions from multiple perspectives rather than relying exclusively on one area of expertise. 2. Supporting evidence-informed policy work The fellowship is also intended to help public and civil servants strengthen their policy work through greater engagement with research. Participants will have an opportunity to examine their policy challenges through a research perspective and identify evidence, tools and resources that could inform their work. This can be particularly valuable for professionals dealing with complex policy issues where decisions require an understanding of data, research findings, evaluation methods and different perspectives. 3. Encouraging professional development The fellowship provides more than access to academics. Participants can use the experience to develop broader professional skills, including research engagement, collaboration, data analysis, evaluation and working across organisational boundaries. The programme therefore offers an opportunity for participants to strengthen skills that can support their careers in government, public institutions and related organisations. 4. Building professional networks Networking is another important component of the programme. EvEx Policy Fellows will have opportunities to connect with other public and civil servants participating in the programme. This can help participants develop professional relationships with people working on different policy challenges and in different parts of the public sector. Over time, these relationships can contribute to a wider community of professionals interested in connecting policy practice with research and academic expertise. This means the fellowship is not described as being restricted exclusively to senior officials or executives. Professionals at different stages of their public-service careers may be able to apply, provided they meet the programme s eligibility requirements. Applications can be submitted in two formats. Individual applications A public or civil servant can apply individually based on a policy challenge they are currently working on. A team-based fellowship could allow participants to engage with academics collectively and use the fellowship period to explore a shared policy question, project or challenge. What Does the EvEx Policy Fellowship Involve? Successful fellows or fellowship teams will spend up to five days in person at a university or universities. These visits will take place during the period: December 2026 to May 2027 The EvEx team will work with fellows to design a programme that reflects their individual or team s requirements. This means that participants should not necessarily expect an identical schedule to every other fellow. Instead, activities will be organised around the policy questions and professional objectives identified by the fellow or fellowship team. The programme may include several activities. 1. Meetings With Academics Fellows will have the opportunity to meet academics and discuss the policy issues they are working on. These discussions can provide participants with access to specialist knowledge and research perspectives relevant to their work. For example, depending on the policy challenge, a fellow could use these conversations to: Explore existing research on a policy issue Understand different academic perspectives Identify relevant evidence Discuss approaches to analysing a policy problem Explore potential evaluation methods Identify research gaps Understand how academic findings could inform policy practice For team applications, the discussions could involve the entire team working with academics to examine a shared policy question or project. 2. This can be particularly useful for policy challenges that cannot be understood through a single academic field. title: Stanford University Linguistics PhD 2027-28: Fully Funded Doctoral Program in the USA — Eligibility, Requirements, Funding and November 18, 2026 Deadline
summary: Stanford University’s Department of Linguistics is accepting applications for its Ph.D. program for the 2027-28 academic year , offering an opportunity for aspiring linguists and researchers to pursue advanced doctoral study at one of the world’s leading universities. The program combines rigorous theoretical work with empirical research, advanced methodological training, individualized academic development, teaching experience, and opportunities to conduct original research across multiple areas of linguistics. The Stanford Linguistics Ph.D. application deadline is November 18, 2026 . The online application opens in late September, and applicants seeking admission for the 2027-28 academic year must submit the complete application and all required supporting materials by the stated deadline. A particularly significant feature of the program is its funding structure. Stanford states that offers of admission to the Linguistics Ph.D. program include funding for the full five years of doctoral study, including tuition and a stipend, regardless of citizenship . This makes the program particularly relevant to students seeking doctoral-level training in linguistics without limiting eligibility to U.S. citizens or permanent residents. Stanford Linguistics PhD 2027-28: Overview The Stanford Department of Linguistics focuses primarily on doctoral education and provides graduate students with substantial flexibility in developing their academic and research directions. The Ph.D. program emphasizes rigorous theoretical research grounded in empirical language data . Students receive broad training in linguistics while developing specialized interests and conducting original research. The department encourages students to work across linguistic subfields and, where appropriate, connect linguistics with neighboring disciplines. Stanford describes its graduate environment as one in which linguistic theory, multiple research methodologies, and computational research interact. Students have opportunities to participate in coursework, research groups, faculty-led projects, workshops, colloquia, reading groups and other academic activities. The department reports receiving approximately 150 Ph.D. applications each year , with an average of approximately 6–7 students admitted . This means applicants should prepare an application that clearly demonstrates their academic preparation, research interests, linguistic background and compatibility with the department’s research environment. Key Details of the Stanford Linguistics PhD Detail Information University Stanford University Department Department of Linguistics Degree Ph.D. in Linguistics Academic Year 2027-28 Study Location Stanford University, California, USA Application Opens Late September 2026 Application Deadline November 18, 2026 Application Fee $125 GRE Not required TOEFL Required for applicants whose first language is not English, subject to Stanford exemptions/waivers Recommendations 3 letters Writing Sample Required Funding Full five-year Ph.D. funding including tuition and stipend Citizenship Ph.D. funding is available regardless of citizenship Program Format Full-time, in-residence doctoral study The application and supporting materials must be submitted online. Stanford does not upload documents sent to the department by email into an applicant s online application. What Does the Stanford Linguistics PhD Offer? The doctoral program is designed for students who want to develop advanced expertise in linguistic theory and research while making original contributions to the field. Students receive training in areas such as: Linguistic theory Empirical linguistic research Research methodology Linguistic description Analytical methods Independent research Academic writing Teaching Dissertation research Interdisciplinary research The program allows students considerable flexibility in choosing coursework and developing their research agenda. Beyond required courses, students can take courses in Linguistics or related departments and may pursue directed reading or research with individual faculty members. Stanford also encourages students to present and publish research and develop professional academic profiles throughout the doctoral program. Stanford Linguistics PhD Program Structure Stanford states that students generally complete the Ph.D. program in five years . The program gradually moves students from broad coursework and foundational training toward specialized independent research and dissertation work. Year 1: Coursework and Research Foundation The first year focuses substantially on coursework in core areas of linguistics. Students select coursework in consultation with faculty advisors to establish a foundation that corresponds to their academic interests and long-term research objectives. The first year may include: Core linguistics coursework A fall seminar introducing students to faculty research Small research groups or individual apprenticeships during the winter quarter Beginning the first qualifying research paper during the spring quarter This structure gives students an opportunity to become familiar with the department s research environment while developing their own research direction. Years 2 and 3: Research Development During the second and third years, the balance gradually shifts from coursework toward research. Students are required to complete two substantial qualifying research papers in different subfields of linguistics . One is completed during the second year and the other during the third year. These qualifying papers are intended to demonstrate the student s ability to conduct independent and original research before beginning the dissertation. By the end of the third year, students select a principal advisor and dissertation committee. Years 4 and 5: Dissertation and Advanced Research The fourth and fifth years are primarily devoted to dissertation research and advanced academic work. The dissertation must demonstrate the student s ability to: Conduct substantial original research Develop and investigate a significant research question Analyze relevant evidence Present research results appropriately for the linguistics community Explain the significance of the research within the broader field of linguistics Students work with a reading committee that provides feedback and guidance throughout the dissertation process. Teaching Experience at Stanford Teaching is an important component of the Stanford Linguistics Ph.D. experience. Doctoral students are required to complete three quarters of teaching by the end of their fourth year , regardless of their source of financial support. Teaching assignments are generally distributed across the second, third and fourth years. Students will generally teach at least one course or assignment related to their primary area of expertise. Stanford also provides access to resources from the university s Vice Provost for Teaching and Learning, including resources available through the Teaching Commons. This teaching component can provide doctoral students with practical experience in university-level instruction in addition to their research training. Research and Academic Opportunities The Stanford Linguistics Ph.D. is not limited to classroom-based study. The program places significant emphasis on original research. Students are encouraged to: Develop independent research projects Conduct empirical investigations Work across linguistic subfields Collaborate with faculty and other researchers Present their work Publish research Participate in research groups Attend colloquia and workshops Engage with neighboring academic disciplines Develop professional academic profiles The department also offers formal and informal opportunities for discussing linguistic research, including colloquia, workshops and reading groups. Stanford s Department of Linguistics also notes opportunities for research and development work through the Center for the Study of Language and Information and, outside the university, with local companies. Eligibility Requirements for Stanford Linguistics PhD Applicants must satisfy Stanford s basic educational eligibility requirements. Applicants must meet one of the following conditions : Hold a bachelor s degree from a U.S. college or university accredited by a regional accrediting association; or Hold an international degree that is equivalent to a U.S. bachelor s degree from a recognized institution. International applicants therefore may apply if their educational qualification meets Stanford s requirements for equivalency to a U.S. bachelor s degree. Academic Background in Linguistics Stanford states that most students admitted to the department have a B.A. or M.A. in Linguistics . However, an applicant does not necessarily need to have completed a degree specifically titled Linguistics. The department occasionally admits applicants whose bachelor s or master s degree is in a related field, provided that they can demonstrate considerable coursework and/or research experience in Linguistics . This means applicants from related academic disciplines should be prepared to demonstrate clearly how their previous academic work has prepared them for advanced linguistic research. What Stanford Looks for in PhD Applicants Stanford uses an individualized and holistic review process rather than relying on a single application component. The department considers factors including: Academic record Letters of recommendation Statement of purpose Personal qualities and characteristics Previous accomplishments Research preparation Understanding of linguistics Motivation to engage in linguistics Research interests Fit between the applicant s interests and the department s faculty expertise Stanford specifically indicates that it looks for evidence of academic potential, understanding of linguistics, strong motivation, passion for research, and compatibility between the applicant s interests and the research strengths of the faculty . Importantly, the department does not specify a minimum GPA for applicants. Stanford states that all components of the application are considered as part of its overall review. Stanford Linguistics PhD Application Requirements Applicants must submit a complete online application along with the required supporting materials. 1. Online Application Form Applicants must complete the Stanford University Graduate Admissions application online. The application is submitted through Stanford s graduate admissions system, and applicants should ensure that all required sections and program-specific materials are completed before the deadline. 2. Application Fee The application fee listed by the Stanford Department of Linguistics is $125 . The department states that it is not able to provide fee waivers directly, while directing applicants to Stanford s university-wide information concerning fee waivers and eligibility. Applicants should therefore review the applicable Stanford Graduate Admissions fee-waiver information if they believe they may qualify. 3. Statement of Purpose The Statement of Purpose is an important part of the application. Stanford asks applicants to use the statement as a narrative presentation of themselves and to clearly address several areas. The statement should explain: Previous Accomplishments Applicants should discuss what they have accomplished so far in linguistics or related fields. This can include relevant academic work, research projects, scholarly activities and other experiences that demonstrate preparation for doctoral study. Why a PhD in Linguistics? Applicants should explain why they want to study linguistics at the doctoral level. The statement should make clear both: Why the applicant wants to study linguistics; and Why pursuing a Ph.D. is necessary or appropriate for achieving their academic or professional goals. Why Stanford? Applicants should explain why Stanford is an appropriate environment for their graduate education. This should connect the applicant s academic and research interests with the opportunities available within Stanford s Linguistics Department. Research Interests Applicants should describe their research interests in linguistics. Applicants whose interests are not yet completely defined can discuss possible research directions and areas they may wish to investigate. A strong statement should therefore do more than provide a general biography. It should demonstrate a logical connection between the applicant s previous preparation, current research interests, doctoral objectives and Stanford s academic environment. 4. GRE Requirement The GRE General Test is not required for admission to Stanford s Department of Linguistics. Stanford also asks applicants who have taken the GRE to refrain from self-reporting their scores in the application. Applicants therefore do not need to take the GRE specifically for the Stanford Linguistics Ph.D. application. 5. TOEFL Requirement for International Applicants The TOEFL is required for applicants whose first language is not English , unless they qualify for an applicable exemption or waiver under Stanford s policies. Applicants who are required to submit TOEFL scores must have their official scores reported directly to Stanford by ETS. Stanford s ETS institutional code is: 4704 Applicants should review Stanford Graduate Admissions current English-language testing requirements to determine whether they qualify for an exemption or waiver and to confirm the applicable minimum-score policies. The Stanford Linguistics Department does not require the Test of Spoken English (TSE) . 6. Official Transcripts Applicants must provide transcripts from all prior college-level institutions attended for at least one year. For the application, applicants submit a scanned copy of the official transcript through the online application system. Applicants should not mail hard-copy transcripts to the Linguistics Department when applying. If Stanford later requires official transcripts, the university will contact the applicant and provide instructions. At that stage, applicants may be asked to provide hard copies or have an electronic transcript sent directly by their degree-granting institution. 7. Three Letters of Recommendation Applicants must submit three letters of recommendation . The letters must be submitted through Stanford s online application system. The Linguistics Department does not accept paper recommendation letters or letters submitted through Interfolio for this application. Stanford recommends selecting recommenders who: Have taught the applicant Have supervised the applicant s research Know the applicant and their academic work well Understand linguistics Can evaluate the applicant s potential for doctoral study Understand what advanced research in linguistics involves Applicants should give recommenders sufficient time to prepare and submit their letters. Stanford notes that late recommendation letters may be submitted, but the department cannot guarantee that materials received after the deadline will be reviewed . 8. Writing Sample A writing sample is required as part of the Stanford Linguistics Ph.D. application. Stanford prefers a writing sample on a linguistics topic, although a paper from another discipline can also be appropriate if it demonstrates the applicant s research ability and writing skills. The purpose of the writing sample is to help the Admissions Committee understand how the applicant: Approaches a research problem Develops a research question Conducts independent research Works through evidence Develops an argument Analyzes information Communicates research in writing Stanford specifically emphasizes that the sample should demonstrate not simply how the applicant writes, but also how the applicant works and thinks as a researcher . Recommended Length A writing sample of approximately 10 to 15 pages is considered standard. A paper in Linguistics is preferred when possible, although Stanford also identifies related fields such as: Logic Anthropology Other relevant disciplines as possible sources for a suitable research paper. Applicants who have completed a B.A. or M.A. thesis may use the thesis as their writing sample. However, applicants should submit only one writing sample and designate no more than 25 pages for the Admissions Committee to focus on. Full Funding for the Stanford Linguistics PhD One of the most important aspects of the opportunity is Stanford s funding commitment. Stanford states that offers of admission to the Linguistics Ph.D. program include funding for the full five years of doctoral study , including: Tuition Stipend The department states that this funding applies regardless of citizenship . This is distinct from applying for a separate external scholarship: Stanford s Linguistics Department states that funding is included with offers of admission to its Ph.D. program. The department nevertheless encourages applicants to pursue external fellowships and scholarships for which they are eligible. Knight-Hennessy Scholars at Stanford Applicants to Stanford s Linguistics Ph.D. may also consider the Knight-Hennessy Scholars (KHS) program. Knight-Hennessy Scholars brings together graduate students from across Stanford s seven graduate schools and provides a multidisciplinary and multicultural leadership-development environment. According to Stanford Linguistics, KHS admits up to 100 applicants each year and provides a leadership program lasting up to three years. KHS also provides full funding for up to three years of Ph.D. studies at Stanford. The program is designed around leadership development and multidisciplinary engagement, giving scholars opportunities to participate in a broader Stanford community beyond their individual academic discipline. Knight-Hennessy Eligibility Stanford states that: Candidates of any country may apply. Applicants must have earned their first undergraduate degree within the previous seven years . Applicants must apply to both a Stanford graduate program and Knight-Hennessy Scholars. Current Stanford Ph.D. students may also apply during their first year of Ph.D. enrollment. The KHS application is separate from the Stanford graduate-program application. Stanford Graduate Admissions confirms that applicants must submit a separate application to be considered for Knight-Hennessy Scholars. Applicants interested in KHS should check the current Knight-Hennessy Scholars application cycle separately for its applicable deadline and requirements. International Students and Applicants From Outside the United States The Stanford Linguistics Ph.D. is open to applicants with qualifying international bachelor s degrees. An international degree can satisfy the educational eligibility requirement when it is equivalent to a U.S. bachelor s degree and was earned from an appropriately recognized institution. The department s Ph.D. funding is also stated to apply regardless of citizenship. For applicants whose first language is not English, TOEFL requirements may apply, although Stanford provides exemptions and waivers under certain circumstances. International applicants should therefore pay particular attention to: Degree equivalency requirements English-language testing requirements Official transcript requirements Recommendation letters Writing sample requirements Stanford s graduate application requirements Immigration and visa procedures after admission Stanford states that international applicants do not need to submit financial verification with the initial admission application. If admitted and accepting an offer, however, international students will need to follow Stanford s process for obtaining the appropriate visa documentation, including providing proof of funding as required. Is the Stanford Linguistics PhD Online or Part-Time? No. Stanford s Linguistics Department states that the Ph.D. program is designed with the expectation that students devote their full time to graduate study and remain in residence for the duration of the program. The department does not offer online or distance-learning instruction in Linguistics for this Ph.D. program. Applicants should therefore be prepared for a full-time, in-person doctoral program at Stanford. Do Applicants Need to Contact Stanford Faculty Before Applying? Stanford states that applicants are not expected to contact faculty members about their availability as a research supervisor before applying . The department s admissions process is not based on a single professor independently selecting students. Instead, applications are initially reviewed by the Admissions Committee, after which the broader department faculty participates in the admissions process. Applicants should nevertheless carefully examine Stanford Linguistics faculty research areas to understand whether their academic interests align with the department. Stanford itself recommends that prospective applicants review faculty and graduate-student research pages and the department s research information when assessing whether the program fits their interests. Important Application Timeline Applicants seeking admission for the 2027-28 academic year should take note of the following key date: Application Opens Late September 2026 Stanford Linguistics PhD Application Deadline November 18, 2026 The entire application and supplemental materials should be submitted online by the deadline. Applicants should not wait until the final day to begin preparing their materials because several components require coordination with other people, particularly recommendation letters and official test-score reporting. A practical preparation sequence would be: Review the eligibility requirements. Research Stanford Linguistics faculty and research areas. Identify potential research interests. Prepare the Statement of Purpose. Select an appropriate writing sample. Request three recommendation letters. Arrange TOEFL testing if required. Collect transcripts. Complete the online application. Review every section and upload all required materials. Submit the application before November 18, 2026 . What Makes the Writing Sample Particularly Important? Because Stanford uses the writing sample to evaluate an applicant s independent research ability, applicants should select a paper that demonstrates genuine analytical and research capacity rather than simply choosing their longest academic assignment. A suitable sample should ideally show: A clearly defined research question An appropriate research methodology Evidence or data Analysis A coherent argument Engagement with relevant academic literature Independent intellectual work Clear academic writing Stanford s description of qualifying research papers provides additional insight into the department s broader expectations for independent research: students are expected to formulate and delimit research questions, develop hypotheses, select appropriate methodologies, collect relevant data, analyze that data and construct a compelling linguistic argument. While the application writing sample and later qualifying papers are not the same requirement, this gives prospective applicants a useful indication of the research-oriented environment they would enter. The department states that students are encouraged to develop active professional profiles, present and publish their research, and make original contributions to knowledge. The combination of: Advanced coursework Independent research Teaching experience Faculty advising Qualifying research papers Dissertation research Research presentations Publication opportunities Interdisciplinary engagement can provide broad preparation for careers involving research, higher education, language-related scholarship, computational or interdisciplinary work, and other professional applications of linguistic expertise. Important Things Applicants Should Remember Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should carefully verify the following: The application is for the Stanford Linguistics Ph.D. The intended entry year is 2027-28 The deadline is November 18, 2026 A qualifying bachelor s degree is required International degrees must meet Stanford s equivalency requirements A Linguistics degree is common but not absolutely mandatory when substantial Linguistics coursework/research can be demonstrated The GRE is not required TOEFL may be required for applicants whose first language is not English Three recommendation letters are required A Statement of Purpose is required A writing sample is required Transcripts are required The application fee is $125 Materials must be submitted online Stanford Linguistics Ph.D. admission offers include five years of funding, including tuition and stipend, regardless of citizenship The Ph.D. is a full-time, in-residence program Applicants do not need to secure a faculty supervisor before applying Knight-Hennessy Scholars requires a separate application KHS is open to candidates from any country, subject to its eligibility requirements How to Apply for the Stanford Linguistics PhD Interested applicants should begin by reviewing Stanford University s official graduate admissions system and the Stanford Department of Linguistics graduate admissions requirements. The application should contain a coherent academic profile showing the applicant s preparation for doctoral research, motivation for studying linguistics, research interests and reasons for applying to Stanford. Particular attention should be given to the Statement of Purpose, recommendation letters and writing sample because these materials provide the department with substantive evidence of the applicant s academic preparation and research potential. Applicants should also verify the latest university-wide requirements before submission, particularly regarding English-language testing, international degree equivalency, application fees and application procedures. Application deadline: November 18, 2026. Conclusion The Stanford University Linguistics Ph.D. for 2027-28 provides an opportunity for students interested in advanced linguistic research to pursue doctoral study in a highly research-oriented academic environment. The program combines theoretical and empirical approaches to linguistics with flexible coursework, independent research, teaching experience and dissertation work. Applicants must hold a qualifying bachelor s degree or equivalent international qualification and should normally have substantial preparation in Linguistics. Candidates from related disciplines may also be considered when they can demonstrate considerable Linguistics coursework and/or research experience. The application requires an online application, $125 application fee, Statement of Purpose, applicable English-language test scores, transcripts, three recommendation letters and a writing sample. The GRE is no longer required. One of the program s most notable features is its funding commitment: Stanford states that admission offers to the Linguistics Ph.D. include five years of funding covering tuition and a stipend, regardless of citizenship . For prospective applicants, preparation should begin well before the deadline. Developing a strong research direction, selecting an effective writing sample, securing thoughtful recommendation letters and preparing a focused Statement of Purpose can all help ensure that the application accurately represents the applicant s academic preparation and research ambitions. The application deadline for students seeking to begin the Stanford Linguistics Ph.D. in the 2027-28 academic year is November 18, 2026 . Prospective applicants should consult Stanford s official admissions pages for the latest requirements before submitting their applications.
